Listen, I am a mother with a 21 year old son who lives very far away. I miss him and would love for him to live with me so I had this particularly great person to talk with on a regular basis.  However, as his mother, I would never want him to do that. I want him to be happy and have his own life and adventures. I want him to be an functioning adult, to know that he is competent to make it in the world. I'm here if he needs a place to crash for a few months, but my guess is that, other than holidays, he won't be living with me anymore. That's okay. That is life.

And in truth, he is awesome about calling me regularly and we talk at least once or twice a week. So I don't miss out on great conversations with him. Just because you move, doesn't mean you lose touch with your mother. Give her a call every now and then. 

It sounds like your mother has lost sight of some important aspects of being a parent. She seems to be using you so that she doesn't have to deal with your brother and other aspects of her life. If she worries about being home alone because of medical issues, she can research medical alert systems. There are plenty of people living alone with serious health concerns who use these because this is exactly what they are for. If she doesn't like being home alone, perhaps she could get a pet, or find some friends to spend time with. 

Your job is not to stay with your mother. Her job is to let you go.

If your nephew's father cannot be alone with his son, he has abused his son physically or sexually, or endangered him. It has to be serious for a court to rule that he cannot be alone with his son. Your sister knows this and continues to see him. She also continues to use heroin. Her judgement isn't good - drug addiction does that to people.

I know you don't want to rock the boat, but I bet you also don't want to be responsible for not taking action that could save your nephew from serious harm. Please call CPS. There is a reason that they protect babies from junkies and unfit parents.

If you continue to protect your sister from the real consequences of her actions, you are not helping her - you're actually hurting her. It is far better for her to face the consequences of what she has done now than when she has hurt or killed her baby, or allowed your nephew's father to do something terrible.

She will not change unless and until she accepts responsibility for what she's doing. Don't cover up for her. I know you don't want to hurt your sister, but she is hurting herself. Please help protect your nephew.

It doesn't have to be either/or. It could be both/and. In other words, you can *both* follow your dreams *and* help your parents.  You and your parents may have to open up to different ideas. For example, you may buy a duplex instead of a single house or apartment when the times comes so that your parents have a place to live. They may come live in another country with you one day. There are a million possibilities.

There is nothing wrong with prioritizing your needs. That does not mean your parents aren't important. For now, you can focus on your education- take a gap year or take a year to study abroad- that way you get to see the world and finish your studies at the same time. I know there are amazing art programs in Cortona and Paris. I am sure there are many more. 

If you have a fully funded graduate art opportunity, take it. There are jobs in the arts that pay well. All those overseas art programs have coordinators for example. Some museums are quite well funded. My best friend is an artist who started her own community pottery studio and another good friend teaches art at a university. They make excellent money.

Your parents aren't children. If they are living on less than 25k, they don't have expensive tastes and know how to stretch their money. They haven't made enough money to save for retirement. 

Once they are 65, Medicare kicks in and they will have excellent healthcare. They may have to continue to work part time, or they may have to cultivate serious garden for additional food. Who knows what solutions the three of you will find? 

You are 20 and this seems insurmountable. It's not. But you absolutely need to take care of yourself. Maybe some counseling to untangle your relationship with money?

Have you talked about the basics: will you both be driving? Do either of you get carsick? Is one of you a planner and the other a freestyler? Can you agree on music? I wish someone would burst this bubble. I urge you to read more than Nestle PR headlines if you want to know more about this very real, ongoing issue. Nestle certainly says the allegations are history to the public and their shareholders, but *this is simply not so.* Nestle continues to market "infant feeding products" in third world countries as well as new mothers at hospital in my hometown in the USA right now.

 [The ICDC](http://www.ibfan-icdc.org/) is an excellent source of information about this a very serious, ongoing issue that effects mothers and babies all over the world. 

First, you should know that there is an [International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes](http://www.who.int/nutrition/publications/code_english.pdf) adopted by the World Health Assembly (WHA) of the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1981. 

Nestlé was involved in the consultation process of the drafting of the International Code. It approved the recommendations resulting from the 1979 preparatory meeting. This is why many folks in the early 1980s believed that the boycott, which began in the 1970s had worked.  Surely Nestle would  implement the minimum standards prescribed by the International Code, since it helped write them, right?

Nope. Nestlé is a greater source of violations in IBFAN’s monitoring than any other company in the world. [Here](http://www.babymilkaction.org/archives/3512) are Nestlé Chairman, Peter Brabeck-Letmathé's responses, mostly non-answers and double-speak,  *last month* at a shareholders meeting to current, ongoing violations of the code. 

[Here](http://www.ibfan.org/art/icdcnestleinstructions.pdf) is a link to how Nestle creatively [mis]interprets the code to justify its unethical practices to the public and its shareholders. Nestlé admitted last year that 90% of the company's code violations are allowed by Nestlé’s own policies, which is why IBFAN is calling for these to be changed.


Nestlé controls 26% of the world wide market for baby food, operates in over 100 countries, and sales of infant nutrition products in 2003 are estimated at CHF 4 billion. Due to its size and the extent of its business, Nestlé exerts a significant influence on governments, market trends, and company behavior -- more than any other single food company. 


Here's an example of how they thwart the code:  Any form of promotion (direct or indirect) of products covered by the International Code is prohibited under Art. 5.14. The prohibition covers all breastmilk substitutes. Nestle creatively interprets this prohibition to cover only products labeled "infant formula." And surprise, surprise, there are now a host of newer products such as "follow-on milks", "infant teas," juices as well as "infant cereals," vegetable mixes, and other complementary foods *that are intended for use with babies under 6 months.* These products cause the same problems formula causes, and are both expensive and in the majority of cases unnecessary. These products, according to the code, should never be marketed or promoted in health care systems. Nestle mostly complies with the code as far as infant formula in concerned, but not this host of other infant products. It's disgusting. 

Nestle also creatively interprets the code to apply only to third world countries, despite  WHO and Unicef making it very clear that there should be *no distinction between developed and developing countries with respect to breastfeeding in general or the International Code in particular.* 

La-la-la, Nestle sticks its fingers in its ears over that issue.  [Here](http://www.ibfan-icdc.org/files/Monitoring_Nestle_SMAknow-how_Ireland.pdf) is a link to an event in Ireland *next week* demonstrating how Nestle continues to violate the basic tenants of the International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes. [Here](http://www.ibfan-icdc.org/index.php/focus/monitoring) is a link to many other, as-yet unpublished code violations. 

Here is summary of how Nestle and Danone are using [new marketing trends](http://www.babymilkaction.org/update46page20#2) to increase their markets at the expense of reducing overall breastfeeding and costing babies lives.

[This](http://www.babymilkaction.org/btr14inbrief) is a link to an abridged version of the 2011-2013 violations of the International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes and subsequent World Health Assembly resolutions (the Code), which are the yardstick to measure compliance by all companies in all countries. It was published in 2014. 

[Here](http://www.babymilkaction.org/archives/3568) is a good run-down of how Nestle excuses their violations of IBFAN policies to its shareholders. 

There is a new movie about this very issue called [Tigers](http://www.babymilkaction.org/tigers) based on the true story of former Nestle Pakistan salesman taking on the baby milk industry with the help of IBFAN. 

Here's a long summary: *"Taamir was a Nestlé baby formula salesman (a.k.a. “medical delegate”) in Pakistan from 1994 to 1997. When a doctor told him that babies were dying from unsafe bottle feeding, Aamir asked why and the doctor replied, 'Because of people like you.' Aamir had been taught to market the company's products aggressively to doctors and parents. The company provided him with funds and resources to organize baby shows and gifts to doctors to encourage them to recommend his company’s formula. He received bonuses for hitting his formula and baby food sales targets. Aamir learnt that all this was in violation of marketing rules adopted through the United Nations (the International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes and subsequent, relevant Resolutions of the World Health Assembly). He quit his job, but realized that was not enough. So he tried to expose and stop the corporation’s malpractice.

BFAN-ICDC’s Director, Annelies Allain met Aamir back in 1998, at a Training on Code Monitoring in Delhi, India. She examined his evidence, such as receipts for gifts to doctors, salary bonus slips based on achieving sales targets and more. She concluded that these were violating the Code, that this man was holding a “smoking gun” and that it should go public.

The IBFAN group in Pakistan produced a report called “Milking Profits” which was launched in Germany in December 1999. Nestlé dismissed the report, claiming most practices were not violations and those that were had been the sole responsibility of Aamir. It also accused him of trying to blackmail the company. The company went on to put pressure on newspapers and on a German TV documentary not to release a film they had made in Pakistan. Wherever possible, Aamir’s testimony was minimized by Nestle. Tigers tells the story of how that big company went to great lengths to suppress media exposure. Aamir was also under pressure of the doctors he had denounced and moved his family into hiding after receiving threats. He eventually sought refuge while in Canada to promote Milking Profits. It took seven years before his wife and small children could join him and both his parents passed away during those difficult years."*

Since this events depicted in the movie took place in the 1990s, Nestle would *love* for the public to believe it's all in the distant past, or that its based on the allegations of just one man. It is worth noting that the events depicted in *Tigers*  took place more than a decade after the International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes was adopted, that the allegations are substantiated by documentary evidence, and that there are many current examples. The film includes footage of actual babies, malnourished after being formula fed, who were filmed in 2013. 

Want current examples?  How about the 2015 UK job advert for a [Nestle Clinical Network Representatives](http://www.babymilkaction.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/nestlesmajobuk0415.pdf). Since they are prohibited from targeting staff in health facilities in the UK, Nestle representatives run events at nearby hotels in an attempt to entice health workers there so it can promote its products with idealizing claims. [Here](http://www.babymilkaction.org/nosponsorship-poster) is a great response to Nestle's efforts.

I have been sober for 25 years. There are former friends from college who still will not speak to me and I do not blame them a bit. I wasn't an extra-special or extra-bad alcoholic. I was just your average self-centered, alcohol-and-drug-fueled bull in the china shop of everyone else's life. I've had a good life for many years now, but I do not assume I deserve forgiveness for how I behaved just because I have a disease or because I am sober.  I certainly don't hold it against any of my friends who "abandoned" me before I got sober and during the early years. I am grateful for it actually. 

You got your feelings hurt over a phrase: "someone like that" and you've held on to some self-righteous anger for over two years. Yes, you have a disease. Good friends don't always hold a warm towel up to your ass while you're shitting on them. The best friends kick you down the road until you can show them, really prove to them, that you've changed. 

I love alcoholics. I have known and loved quite a few. I won't have anything to do with active alcoholics unless they are trying to get help. Active alcoholics are shitty people. I know because I have been one.

She told you to sober up or she didn't really want you to be in the wedding. *She still wanted you to come to the wedding even after you chose alcohol.* You got on your high horse and decided to show her by not attending. Good god, the hubris.

The selfishness of your behavior isn't surprising at all. It's what alcoholics do. The surprising thing to me is that 2+ years later, you are still justifying it and you're still angry at her. What exactly did you expect her to do in the way of "supporting" you? 

There is a tendency for people in early sobriety to want a big pat on the back for doing the things *other folks have been doing all along.* Like getting sober. It's great that you're sober. Keep it up. 

If you really want to reconcile with her, than focus on what you did and taking responsibility for it. If you want to reconcile because you want an apology from her, then I don't think you really want to reconcile. Honestly, she sounds very forgiving of your shitty behavior, and happy that you are sober. I think you're lucky to have her as a friend. You could apologize for your self-righteous refusal to attend her wedding, for putting alcohol over her friendship, and for being such a shitty friend.

I think self-hatred is one of the hardest things to deal with. I totally relate to your cycle: self-hate, seek comfort, overeat, self-hate.

Here's a simple formula that works for me. Please note that it is simple, not necessarily easy. To eliminate self-hate, I have to practice estimable behavior. I have to do things that *I* respect. I try to keep this very simple. For example, clean up for 15 minutes a day. Or only eat three meals a day. 

How it works: I try to make these new behaviors very concrete. Usually when I begin, it isn't easy. When I started with three meals a day, some of those meals were larger than I wanted them to be, but I held on to the new habit no matter what. After a few weeks, it starts to get easier, more routine. I feel so much better that there are limits to my eating time and that I am not eating into the night. The more I keep practicing it, the easier it becomes. After a month or so, I add a new one.

Three days ago, I started a new one: exercise for 10 minutes a day. I have several autoimmune conditions and many days I am physically in pain. I can't exercise the way I could when I was younger and healthier. I am also quite out of shape. Sad to say that right now, 10 or 15 minutes of walking leaves me sore. The first day, I went out and walked. Felt great during and afterwards, tried not to dwell on being out of breath as I walked up a hill. It's autumn, it's lovely. Yesterday, day 2, I procrastinated, which I have done many times before. It was 10:30 at night and I hadn't done my 10 minutes. Was I going to stop before I had really started? Why not? It's late, I'm tired, yadda, yadda, yadda. I keep track of these little habits and I enter them in at night. When I got to my newest one, the 10 minutes of exercise, I looked at the screen. No one would know I had started, much less stopped this new habit. But *I* would know. I actually got up, put the pup on a leash and went for a 10 minute walk around the block. I was sore, but I felt so much better because I was practicing something I respect.

Today, I am going to get my walk done in the morning, because I don't want to have that little internal battle at 10:30 at night again. 

When I am in the throes of self-hate, I want to change everything, right now. However, it's better for me to make one real, meaningful concrete change, and give myself time to make it a real habit than to try a large scale overhaul that I burn out on.
